extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of periodical/satirical essays (early-18th-century literate public); dramatists and critics interested in comedy, character, and moral satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing short, moralizing satirical/humorous essays and dramatic characters that instruct as well as amuse, using allegory, concrete detail, and classical allusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose in comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets (playwrights) should catch at men's hearts to their good and advantage, attempting it 'with the Honesty which becomes their Characters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make comic characters and plots serve a reforming or instructive end: show vice in a way that leads the audience to better judgment (e.g., present agreeable characters who also exemplify virtue so they may 'smite and reprove the Heart of a Man of Sense'). Avoid mere buffoonery that lacks ethical consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spurious oaths and coarse force in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's plays 'absolutely discard[ed] the customary way of enforcing feeble dialogues by the spurious force of oaths, and aim[ed] at a wholesome influence upon his audience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on coarse swearing or cheap shocks to give weight to dialogue; prefer cleaner, purposed speech that supports the play's humane/moral aims and keeps the tone suitable to instruct as well as amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make virtuous characters agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: A man that is temperate, generous, valiant, chaste, faithful and honest may, at the same time, have wit, humour, mirth, good-breeding, and gallantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray virtuous qualities alongside wit and liveliness so that comic pleasure reinforces admiration for goodness. Create occasions in the narrative to show how the character's wit coexists with—and reveals—their higher virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single dominant vice for believable characters
rubrics_metrics.description: There is seldom a Person devoted to above one Darling Vice at a time, so that there is room enough to catch at Men's Hearts...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For credible satire and comic effect, give characters one central failing rather than piling on many vices. That concentrated flaw is easier to lampoon and to use for moral contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plot outcomes to expose vice (catastrophe/retribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Might not such a one divert the Audience quite as well, if at the Catastrophe he were found out for a Traitor, and met with Contempt accordingly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure dramatic or satirical plots so that characters' vices are exposed and judged by the denouement; moral reckoning at the catastrophe strengthens the instructive dimension of comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct laughter at foolish characters, not the author
rubrics_metrics.description: When readers laughed at the paper, they 'laughed at the Idiot, the German Courtier, the Gaper, the Merry-Andrew, the Haberdasher, the Biter, the Butt, and not at' the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure comic targets are clearly the foolish characters or social follies; the authorial voice should preserve dignity so the audience laughs at the object of satire rather than viewing the author as ridiculed or merely buffoonish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate the audience as a route to social improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: To embellish the Mistress, you should give a new Education to the Lover, and teach the Men not to be any longer dazzled by false Charms and unreal Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When social satire aims to improve manners, consider addressing or reshaping the audience's perceptions (e.g., men’s tastes) rather than only mocking the immediate subjects; comic persuasion can aim at changing admirers' values to reward virtue over superficial charms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ allegory and fable to dramatize abstract faults
rubrics_metrics.description: I threw my Thoughts into a little kind of Allegory or Fable ... two powerful Tyrants, Luxury and Avarice, their Generals and Privy-Counsellors (Poverty, Plenty) who negotiate and finally share conquests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personify abstract qualities (Luxury, Avarice, etc.), give them relationships and quarrels, and let their interactions dramatize moral analysis. Allegory lets readers grasp complex social/moral dynamics through narrative and personified conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid, concrete details and quotidian observation in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lowngers can tell every time any Butcher kills a Calf, every time any old Woman's Cat is in the Straw; one contemplates two or three Hours every Day over a Sun-Dial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground satire in specific, observable behaviors and local color—small, recognizable facts and routines make mockery sharper and funnier. Catalogue particulars of habit and place to build credibility and comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical allusion and learned citations as rhetorical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The essays repeatedly cite classical authors (Virgil, Horace, Persius, Sallust, Epictetus) and use translations/quotations to frame topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke classical quotations and authorities to lend weight, irony, or contrast to a humorous point. Such allusions can both elevate the piece and provide a learned foil for satirizing contemporary manners—use them strategically to enrich tone.
